messages.content: Get me this coming Saturday's weather forecast?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content: Sure! To give you an accurate forecast, could you let me know where you'd like the weather information for? You can share a city name or your latitude and longitude.
message.reasoning:
The user wants the weather forecast for "this coming Saturday". We need to determine the date of the upcoming Saturday relative to today. Today is 2026-07-28. Let's find the next Saturday after that date.

We can compute the day of week for July 28, 2026. But we can also just calculate manually: 2026-07-28 is a Thursday? Let's check quickly: 2026-01-01 is a Friday? Actually let's do a quick calculation: 2026-01-01 is a Friday? Wait, 2025-01-01 was a Wednesday? Let's not rely on memory. Instead, we can approximate: 2026-07-28 is likely a Thursday. But we can confirm: 2026-07-28 is indeed a Thursday. So the next Saturday would be two days later: 2026-07-30. So we want the forecast for 2026-07-30.

We need to call the function `requests_get` with the appropriate URL. The Open-Meteo API endpoint for forecast: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast". We need to provide query parameters: latitude, longitude, elevation optional, timezone, daily variables like temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min, precipitation_sum, windspeed_10m_max, etc. Also we need to specify start_date and end_date as 2026-07-30. We might also want to set hourly or daily. For a simple forecast, we can use daily variables. We'll set daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min,precipitation_sum,windspeed_10m_max. And we need to set timezone=auto or maybe specify a timezone. We can set timezone=auto to get local time zone based on lat/lon. Or we can set timezone=UTC. But auto is fine.

We need to decide which location. The user didn't specify a location. We could ask them for their location. But the instruction says: "If you don't know the answer, ask clarifying questions." So we should ask for the user's location. But we can also guess a default location like New York City. But better to ask. So we will ask: "Could you please tell me your location (city or coordinates) so I can fetch the forecast?" That is the best approach.

Thus we will respond asking for clarification.
